## Back to Unit K

In [Unit K](un_K.html) we used two [quantitative]{.blue} explanatory variables,
the diameter and the height of the black cherry trees. In this unit we
include also [qualitative]{.orange} explanatory variables.

## A qualitative explanatory variable

Let us go back to the `Houses` data of [Exercises B](exe/exe_B.html): the
selling price (`price`, thousands of dollars) and the size (`size`, square
feet) of $100$ houses, and whether the house is new (`new`, $1 =$ yes,
$0 =$ no).

```{r}
path <- "https://stat4ds.rwth-aachen.de/data/Houses.dat"
Houses <- read.table(path, header = TRUE)
Houses$new <- factor(Houses$new, levels = c(0, 1), labels = c("no", "yes"))
```

::: callout-note
#### Research question

Are new houses more expensive than old ones? By how much?
:::

A qualitative variable can be included in `lm` as any other variable:

```{r}
fit_new <- lm(price ~ new, data = Houses)
coef(fit_new)
```

**R** creates the [indicator]{.blue} variable `newyes`, equal to $1$ for new
houses and $0$ for old ones. Denoting it by $x_i$, the model is the simple
linear regression model of [Unit K](un_K.html), $$
Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i + \epsilon_i,
$$ so that $\beta_0$ is the mean price of old houses ($x_i = 0$) and
$\beta_0 + \beta_1$ is the mean price of new houses ($x_i = 1$). Therefore,
$\beta_1$ is the [difference]{.orange} between the mean prices of new and old
houses. The first category, `no`, is the
[reference category]{.blue}: it has no indicator. With $c$ categories, **R**
creates $c - 1$ indicators, one for each category except the first.

```{r}
price_no <- Houses$price[Houses$new == "no"]
price_yes <- Houses$price[Houses$new == "yes"]
mean(price_no)
mean(price_yes) - mean(price_no)
```

## Adjusting for the size

New houses are, however, also [larger]{.orange}:

```{r}
boxplot(size ~ new, data = Houses)
```

Let us compare new and old houses [of the same size]{.blue}, with the model
$Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{i1} + \beta_2 x_{i2} + \epsilon_i$, where $x_{i1}$ is
the size and $x_{i2}$ is the indicator of new houses. Now $\beta_2$ is the
difference between the mean prices of new and old houses, at fixed size:

```{r}
fit_size_new <- lm(price ~ size + new, data = Houses)
summary(fit_size_new)
```

At fixed size, a new house costs on average $87$ thousand dollars more than
an old one, and not $229$: a large part of the difference between the two
groups is due to the size. The difference remains statistically significant
(P-value $0.003$).

This is the same phenomenon seen with the trees in [Unit K](un_K.html): the effect of a variable
changes when another variable, related to both, enters the model. The size is
a [confounding variable]{.orange} for the comparison between new and old
houses.

::: callout-warning
These are [observational]{.blue} data: association does not imply causation.
Adjusting for the size removes its effect, but other variables that are not in
the data (the neighbourhood, the quality of the materials, ...) could still
explain part of the difference.
:::

## Diagnostic plots for the `Houses` data

As in [Unit K](un_K.html), we check the assumptions of the model with the first
two diagnostic plots:

```{r}
par(mfrow = c(1, 2)) # Two plots side by side
plot(fit_size_new, which = 1:2)
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

-   `Residuals vs Fitted`: the cloud is [fan-shaped]{.orange}, since the
    residuals are more spread out for the more expensive houses. The variance
    is therefore not constant. House $64$, the largest one, has a very negative
    residual: its price is much lower than predicted from its size.
-   `Q-Q Residuals`: in the upper part, the points lie clearly above the dotted
    line. The distribution of the residuals is [skewed to the right]{.orange},
    as the prices themselves in [Exercises B](exe/exe_B.html).

The normality and constant variance assumptions are therefore questionable: the
estimates are still meaningful, but the P-values and the intervals should be
taken as [approximate]{.blue}.

## Comparing three groups

The `Income` data file of @Agresti2022 reports, for $n = 80$ adult Americans
aged over 25, the annual income (`income`, thousands of dollars), the number of
years of education (`education`) and the racial-ethnic group (`race`: `B` for
Black, `H` for Hispanic, `W` for White).

::: callout-note
#### Research question

Does the mean income differ among the three groups?
:::

```{r}
path <- "https://stat4ds.rwth-aachen.de/data/Income.dat"
Income <- read.table(path, header = TRUE)
Income$race <- factor(Income$race)
table(Income$race)
boxplot(income ~ race, data = Income)
```

With $c = 3$ categories, **R** creates $c - 1 = 2$ indicators, `raceH` and
`raceW`, and the first category, `B`, is the reference:

```{r}
fit_race <- lm(income ~ race, data = Income)
summary(fit_race)
```

The model is $Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{i1} + \beta_2 x_{i2} + \epsilon_i$, where
$x_{i1}$ and $x_{i2}$ are the indicators of Hispanics and Whites. Denoting by
$\mu_B$, $\mu_H$ and $\mu_W$ the mean incomes of the three groups, we have
$\beta_0 = \mu_B$, $\beta_1 = \mu_H - \mu_B$ and $\beta_2 = \mu_W - \mu_B$.
Indeed, the estimates are the differences between the sample means:

```{r}
income_B <- Income$income[Income$race == "B"]
income_H <- Income$income[Income$race == "H"]
income_W <- Income$income[Income$race == "W"]
c(mean(income_B), mean(income_H), mean(income_W))
c(mean(income_H) - mean(income_B), mean(income_W) - mean(income_B))
```

## The analysis of variance

The three groups have the same mean if $H_0: \mu_B = \mu_H = \mu_W$, that is,
if $H_0: \beta_1 = \beta_2 = 0$. This is exactly the hypothesis of the
[F test]{.orange} in the last line of `summary(fit_race)`, also obtained with the
command `anova`:

```{r}
anova(fit_race)
```

This table is called [analysis of variance]{.blue} (ANOVA), because the test
compares two sources of variability:

-   the row `race` measures the variability [between]{.orange} the groups, that
    is, how far the three sample means are from each other;
-   the row `Residuals` measures the variability [within]{.blue} the groups. Its
    `Mean Sq` is $s^2$, the estimate of $\sigma^2$, with $n - 3 = 77$ degrees of
    freedom.

The `F value` is the ratio of the two `Mean Sq`, $1676.24 / 394.93 = 4.24$.
The P-value is $0.018$: there is evidence that [at least two]{.orange} mean
incomes differ. In the table `Coefficients` of `summary(fit_race)`, the
difference between Whites and Blacks is significant (P-value $0.012$), while the
one between Hispanics and Blacks is not (P-value $0.656$). Comparing all the
pairs of groups would require some additional care (*multiple comparisons*),
which is beyond the scope of this unit.

## Adjusting for education

As in [Unit K](un_K.html), we can add a quantitative variable to the model:

```{r}
fit_race_edu <- lm(income ~ race + education, data = Income)
summary(fit_race_edu)
```

-   Each additional year of education corresponds, on average, to $4.43$
    thousand dollars of additional income, adjusting for the group.
-   Adjusting for education, the difference between the mean incomes of Whites
    and Blacks is $10.9$ thousand dollars, instead of $14.7$: part of the
    difference between the groups is due to education.

## Diagnostic plots for the `Income` data

```{r}
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(fit_race_edu, which = 1:2)
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

The red line of `Residuals vs Fitted` is roughly flat, but two people, numbers
$67$ and $72$, have incomes much higher than predicted. In the `Q-Q Residuals`
plot, the points in the upper part lie above the dotted line: as is typical for
incomes, the residuals are [skewed to the right]{.orange}. Also here, the
P-values should be taken as approximate.
